chapter.name: The Parliamentary System: Legislature and Executive

questions.q: On their school trip to Delhi, the Grade 8 students noticed the shape of the new Parliament building. How did they describe it?
questions.a: Like a soft triangle
o: Like a soft triangle
Square, with four equal sides
Round, like a wheel
Six-sided, like a hexagon

questions.q: Which description of the Parliament matches the Introduction of the chapter?
questions.a: The supreme legislative body, which makes the country's laws and guides the government
o: The supreme legislative body, which makes the country's laws and guides the government
The branch of government that interprets laws and settles disputes through a system of courts
A permanent group of officials who work under the direction of ministers in government departments
A body whose only work is to elect the President and the Vice President of India

questions.q:
Answer from the Introduction of the chapter.
(a) Whom do the people of India elect directly, and to which House?
(b) Who, from among those elected, forms the government?
questions.a: (a) The people directly elect their representatives, who become members of the Lok Sabha. (b) A majority group from among these elected representatives forms the government.
s: (a) The people directly elect representatives who become members of the Lok Sabha
(b) A majority group from among the elected representatives forms the government

questions.q: True or false: The new Parliament building, Sansad Bhavan, was constructed to accommodate growing needs including capacity, technology, sustainability and safety. Give the reason for your answer.
questions.a: True. The chapter says the new building in New Delhi was built for these growing needs; the old building, now Samvidhan Sadan, dates from the 1920s and had served as Parliament House for over seven decades.
s: States the verdict: True
Reason: the chapter gives these four growing needs as the purpose of the new building, which replaced one in use for over seven decades

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The government in India can be seen as functioning with the people's consent.
Reason (R): A majority group from among the representatives whom the people directly elect to the Lok Sabha forms the government.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true

questions.q:
Read the statements about India's two Parliament buildings.
I. The Constituent Assembly met for its deliberations in the building now called Samvidhan Sadan.
II. The new Sansad Bhavan was constructed in the 1920s.
III. The old building served as Parliament House for over seven decades.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: I and III only
o: I and III only
I and II only
II and III only
I, II and III

questions.q:
A housing society in Nagpur has 240 adult residents. Its managing committee proposes that, for next year's committee election, only residents who own their flats may vote. Of the 240 adults, 96 live in rented flats. One resident objects at the meeting: 'This is not how our country chooses the members of its Lok Sabha.'
(a) Name the principle, laid down by the Constitution, that gives every adult citizen the right to vote.
(b) Name any two things which, according to the chapter, cannot be used to deny an adult citizen this right.
(c) How many adults would lose their vote under the proposal, and what percentage of all 240 adults is that?
(d) The chapter says the government functions with the people's consent because the people elect their representatives. Explain in one line why a committee chosen under this proposal could not claim the consent of all the residents.
questions.a: (a) Universal Adult Franchise. (b) Any two of: social background, economic background, gender, race, religion. (c) 96 adults; 96 / 240 x 100 = 40 per cent. (d) Two in every five adults would have had no say in choosing it, so it would rest on the consent of only the flat-owners, not of all residents.
s: (a) Universal Adult Franchise
(b) Any two of social or economic background, gender, race, religion
(c) 96 adults, which is 40 per cent of 240
(d) The 96 tenants (40 per cent) had no say, so the committee rests on the consent of owners only

questions.q: By which other name does the chapter call the Rajya Sabha?
questions.a: The Council of States
o: The Council of States
The House of the People
The Legislative Assembly
The Legislative Council

questions.q: During a heated debate in the Lok Sabha, several members speak at once and one member keeps ignoring the rules. According to the chapter, whose job is it to restore order, and how did that person get the post?
questions.a: The Speaker, whom the members of the Lok Sabha elect
o: The Speaker, whom the members of the Lok Sabha elect
The Vice President, who chairs the Lok Sabha by office
The Prime Minister, as leader of the majority in the House
The President, who summons the Parliament

questions.q:
Match each term in Column I with its meaning in the chapter, given in Column II.
Column I: I. Bicameral  II. Sengol  III. Speaker  IV. Federalism
Column II: A. Power distributed between the centre, states and local governments  B. A gold-plated silver sceptre placed near the Speaker's chair  C. A structure of the legislature with two houses  D. The presiding officer elected by Lok Sabha members
questions.a: I-C, II-B, III-D, IV-A
o: I-C, II-B, III-D, IV-A
I-A, II-B, III-D, IV-C
I-C, II-D, III-B, IV-A
I-D, II-B, III-C, IV-A

questions.q:
(a) Break the word 'bicameral' into its two parts and give the meaning of each, as the chapter does.
(b) Why is the Indian Parliament called bicameral?
questions.a: (a) 'Bi' means two and 'cameral' means chamber or house. (b) Besides the President, it has two houses, the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha.
s: (a) 'Bi' = two, 'cameral' = chamber or house
(b) It has two houses, the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha

questions.q:
The chapter says India's parliamentary system has several roots. Answer briefly.
(a) Which country's system inspired India's system of parliamentary democracy?
(b) What ancient republics did the Constitution makers remember?
(c) In the village panchayats, who made the collective decisions?
questions.a: (a) Britain. (b) The ancient republics called mahajanapadas. (c) The elders of the village.
s: (a) Britain
(b) The mahajanapadas
(c) The elders

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The composition and process of election to the Rajya Sabha were designed to be different from those of the Lok Sabha.
Reason (R): The Rajya Sabha is presided over by a Speaker whom its own members elect.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: A is true, but R is false
o: A is true, but R is false
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is false, but R is true

questions.q:
You are a student guide for visitors to the Lok Sabha chamber in the new Parliament building. Write one line for each point of your talk.
(a) The two other names of the Lok Sabha.
(b) How its members are chosen.
(c) The maximum number of members the Constitution envisages for it.
(d) Who presides over it, and any two things that person does.
(e) The sceptre placed near that person's chair, and the figure at its top with what it stands for.
questions.a: (a) The House of the People, or the Lower House. (b) By direct election based on universal adult suffrage. (c) 550. (d) The Speaker, elected by the members; any two of: conducts the sessions, allows members to speak, maintains discipline, ensures that rules are followed. (e) The Sengol; Nandi sits at its top, symbolising justice.
s: (a) House of the People / Lower House
(b) Direct election based on universal adult suffrage
(d) The Speaker, with two of: conducts sessions, lets members speak, keeps discipline, ensures rules are followed
(e) The Sengol, with Nandi at the top symbolising justice

questions.q: The Constitution's key functions of the Parliament are classified under four heads. Which of these is NOT one of them?
questions.a: Settling disputes
o: Settling disputes
Lawmaking
Executive accountability
Financial accountability

questions.q: From among whom is the Council of Ministers chosen, according to the chapter?
questions.a: The MPs of both houses of Parliament
o: The MPs of both houses of Parliament
The MPs of the Lok Sabha only
The civil servants of the ministries
The members of the State Assemblies

questions.q: True or false: The election of the President and the Vice President, and amendments to the Constitution, are constitutional functions of the Parliament. Give the reason for your answer.
questions.a: True. The chapter calls these vital constitutional functions of the Parliament, and adds that there are other important ones to be explored in higher grades.
s: States the verdict: True
Reason: the chapter names both as vital constitutional functions of the Parliament

questions.q:
Read the statements about the core values of the Constitution that the Parliament is entrusted with upholding.
I. Enabling parliamentary democracy through universal adult suffrage is one of them.
II. Following the separation of powers between the legislature, executive and judiciary is one of them.
III. Keeping all power with the centre, so that the states have none, is one of them.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: I and II only
o: I and II only
II and III only
I and III only
I, II and III

questions.q:
An imagined law (illustrative) requires every factory to treat its waste water before releasing it into a river. Two years later, factories in one district still release untreated water and no official has checked them.
(a) Which function of the Parliament was performed when the law was passed?
(b) Which responsibility of the Parliament has not been met in this district?
(c) Use this case to explain why the chapter says the executive responsibility is as important as the legislative function.
questions.a: (a) The legislative function, the making of laws. (b) The executive responsibility, ensuring that laws are implemented and enforced. (c) The law exists on paper but the river is still polluted, because nobody carried it out; the chapter says the Union Executive gives life to the Parliament's legislative power, and without enforcement a law changes nothing.
s: (a) Legislative function: making the law
(b) Executive responsibility: implementing and enforcing it
(c) A law not enforced changes nothing; the Executive gives life to the legislative power

questions.q:
An imagined MP (illustrative) keeps a diary of one week in Parliament. Monday: votes in the election of the Vice President. Tuesday: in the first hour of the session, asks the Health Minister why a hospital scheme has been delayed. Wednesday: examines, with other MPs, how funds have been distributed to different ministries. Thursday: votes on an amendment to the Constitution. Friday: votes on amendments to a bill, clause by clause. A reporter writes that she 'did only one day of Parliament's real work, lawmaking'.
(a) Under which head of the Parliament's functions do Monday and Thursday fall?
(b) Under which head does Tuesday fall?
(c) Under which head does Wednesday fall?
(d) Judge the reporter's remark, using the four heads and the chapter's view of the executive responsibility.
questions.a: (a) Constitutional functions. (b) Executive accountability, through the Question Hour. (c) Financial accountability. (d) The remark is wrong: lawmaking is only one of the four heads the Constitution lays down, and the other four days carried out the other three; the chapter says the executive responsibility is as important as the legislative function, so holding ministers and their spending to account is also Parliament's real work.
s: (a) Constitutional functions
(b) Executive accountability (Question Hour)
(c) Financial accountability
(d) Rejects the remark: all four heads are Parliament's work and the executive responsibility is as important as lawmaking

questions.q: What is a 'bill', as the chapter defines it?
questions.a: A draft of a proposed law that needs the Parliament's approval before it can become law
o: A draft of a proposed law that needs the Parliament's approval before it can become law
An official government publication that announces legal documents and official information
A permanent committee of MPs that scrutinises government activities and makes recommendations
A part of a law that explains its specific details, such as the age group it applies to

questions.q: The RTE bill was tabled in the Rajya Sabha. Suppose it had been tabled in the Lok Sabha instead. In the flowchart of lawmaking, where would the step 'process repeated in other House' then have taken place?
questions.a: In the Rajya Sabha
o: In the Rajya Sabha
In the Lok Sabha, a second time
In a Vidhan Sabha of each state
Nowhere, as the bill would go straight to the President

questions.q: Speaking as RTE, the chapter lists what the Act has done for children today. Name any two of these things.
questions.a: Any two of: it has enabled the creation of legal pathways for children to attend school; it has facilitated new school construction; it has ensured free books and uniforms for children.
s: Names one of: legal pathways to attend school, new school construction, free books and uniforms
Names a second, different one of these

questions.q:
Describe in one line each what happened to RTE at these points in its journey.
(a) Six years after the 86th Constitutional Amendment Act.
(b) In the committee that studied it.
(c) In August 2009.
questions.a: (a) It was tabled as a bill in the Rajya Sabha. (b) The committee studied it thoroughly and suggested modifications; the major debate was over funding new schools, infrastructure and teachers. (c) It was passed in the Lok Sabha and received the President's assent, becoming an Act.
s: (a) Tabled as a bill in the Rajya Sabha
(b) Studied thoroughly by a committee, which suggested modifications
(c) Passed in the Lok Sabha and got the President's assent, becoming an Act

questions.q:
Read the statements about how bills are handled in the Parliament.
I. Every bill must be referred to a Standing Committee before it is voted on.
II. A Money Bill, concerned with matters such as taxation and government borrowing, can be introduced only in the Lok Sabha.
III. The introduction of a Money Bill requires the prior recommendation of the President.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: II and III only
o: II and III only
I and II only
I and III only
I, II and III

questions.q:
An imagined Clean Rivers Bill (illustrative) has 14 clauses. It is introduced in the Rajya Sabha and read, and is then sent to a Standing Committee, which takes five months and suggests 23 changes. In the clause-by-clause discussion, MPs vote to accept 9 of them, including a change to the clause that fixes the fine for polluting. The bill is then passed by a vote in the Rajya Sabha. One MP complains that the committee stage wasted five months and should be skipped for such bills.
(a) What kind of body is a Standing Committee, as the chapter defines it?
(b) What is a clause of a bill?
(c) Name, in order, the three steps of the flowchart still left for this bill.
(d) Should the committee stage be skipped for bills like this? Give a judgement using the flowchart's note and the RTE story.
questions.a: (a) A permanent committee of MPs (the MPs may change but the committee remains) that scrutinises government activities, makes recommendations and asks questions on actions taken. (b) A part of a bill that explains its specific details, such as the fine for polluting here. (c) The process is repeated in the other House (the Lok Sabha), then presidential assent, then gazette notification. (d) The flowchart notes that all bills may not be referred to committees, so skipping is allowed; but the RTE committee studied that bill thoroughly and suggested modifications, and here 9 changes were accepted, so for a detailed bill like this one the five months improved it. A reasoned judgement either way that uses both points earns the mark.
s: (a) A permanent committee of MPs that scrutinises government activities and makes recommendations
(b) A part of a bill explaining its specific details
(c) Process repeated in the Lok Sabha, presidential assent, gazette notification, in that order
(d) Reasoned judgement using both the note that not all bills go to committees and the committee's value in the RTE story

questions.q:
An imagined School Bus Safety Bill (illustrative) is introduced in the Lok Sabha, read, discussed clause by clause and passed by a vote there. Using the chapter's flowchart of lawmaking, answer:
(a) In which House is the process then repeated?
(b) What is the next step after that, and who performs it?
(c) What is the final step, and what is a gazette?
(d) If the bill had been only about a new tax, in which House alone could it have been introduced?
questions.a: (a) In the Rajya Sabha. (b) Presidential assent, given by the President. (c) Gazette notification; a gazette is an official government publication that announces legal documents and official information. (d) In the Lok Sabha, since a Money Bill can be introduced only there.
s: (a) The Rajya Sabha
(b) Presidential assent, by the President
(c) Gazette notification, with the meaning of a gazette
(d) The Lok Sabha only, as a Money Bill

questions.q: When is the Question Hour in the Lok Sabha typically held?
questions.a: In the first hour of a Parliamentary session
o: In the first hour of a Parliamentary session
In the last hour of each sitting day
In the hour after the Union Budget is presented
In the hour when bills are put to the vote

questions.q: In the Question Hour, an MP asks a minister why an imagined highway project (illustrative) has cost twice its estimate. The minister replies: 'That is the government's business, not the House's.' Which idea of the chapter does this reply ignore?
questions.a: The Executive is accountable: it must justify its actions and decisions to the Lok Sabha
o: The Executive is accountable: it must justify its actions and decisions to the Lok Sabha
The Judiciary must check that every law passed by Parliament fits the Constitution
The Council of Ministers is chosen from the MPs of both houses of Parliament
A Money Bill can be introduced only in the Lok Sabha with the President's recommendation

questions.q:
Answer about financial accountability.
(a) Through what does the Parliament approve and monitor government expenditure?
(b) What is the government expected to provide to the Parliament, and in what manner?
questions.a: (a) Through the annual budget, and by examining the distribution of funds to different ministries. (b) The necessary information, in a timely and accurate manner.
s: (a) The annual budget and examining the distribution of funds to ministries
(b) Necessary information, given in a timely and accurate manner

questions.q:
Match each event in Column I with the part of the system it shows, in Column II.
Column I: I. An MP asks the Railway Minister in the first hour of a session why a train service was cut.  II. Ministry officers explain their policy at a meeting of MPs from several parties.  III. MPs examine how funds were distributed among ministries.  IV. The government carries out the budget that Parliament approved.
Column II: A. Financial accountability  B. The Executive's own role  C. The Question Hour  D. A special committee
questions.a: I-C, II-D, III-A, IV-B
o: I-C, II-D, III-A, IV-B
I-D, II-C, III-A, IV-B
I-C, II-D, III-B, IV-A
I-A, II-D, III-C, IV-B

questions.q:
A Standing Committee on Health and Family Welfare recommended that the Ministry of Ayush persuade the States and UTs that have no separate Department of Ayush to create one. The government's Action Taken reply said that public health is a state subject, that the Ministry had requested State/UT governments in meetings to create separate Directorates, and that a separate Ayush Directorate is available in 24 States/UTs.
(a) Why could the Ministry not create these departments itself?
(b) What did the Ministry do instead?
(c) Does this exchange show the Executive being held accountable? Explain, using the committee's role.
questions.a: (a) Public health is a state subject, so creating such a department is for each State/UT government to decide. (b) It requested the State/UT governments in different meetings to create separate Directorates; 24 States/UTs now have one. (c) Yes: the Ministry had to report the action it took and justify why it did not do more, which is what being accountable means; and since a Standing Committee asks questions on actions taken, it can keep checking on the States/UTs not yet covered.
s: (a) Public health is a state subject
(b) It requested States/UTs in meetings to create Directorates; 24 have one
(c) Yes: the Ministry had to report and justify its action to a committee that keeps asking about actions taken

questions.q:
In an imagined year (illustrative), Parliament approves Rs 840 crore for a ministry to build 60 hostels for schoolgirls. At the end of the year the ministry reports that it has spent Rs 630 crore and built 45 hostels.
(a) What percentage of the approved money has been spent?
(b) What percentage of the planned hostels has been built?
(c) Under which head of the Parliament's functions do MPs examine this spending?
(d) Name two ways, given in the chapter, in which MPs can make the ministry explain the unbuilt hostels.
(e) An MP says: 'Spending and building are both at 75 per cent, so Parliament need not ask anything more.' Evaluate this view.
questions.a: (a) 630 / 840 x 100 = 75 per cent. (b) 45 / 60 x 100 = 75 per cent. (c) Financial accountability. (d) The Question Hour, and meetings of special committees where ministries must explain and answer questions. (e) Partly reasonable: money and work have moved together, which suggests no waste so far. But 15 hostels and Rs 210 crore remain, and the Parliament's job is to monitor expenditure and receive timely and accurate information, so it should still ask why the 15 are unfinished and how the rest will be used.
s: (a) 75 per cent spent
(b) 75 per cent built
(c) Financial accountability
(d) Question Hour and special committee meetings
(e) Weighs the matching shares against the 15 unbuilt hostels and Rs 210 crore left, and concludes Parliament should still ask

questions.q: In the Lok Sabha, a minister refuses to answer an MP and says: 'My ministry answers only to the President, not to this House.' True or false: the minister is right. Give the reason or the correct statement.
questions.a: False. The Prime Minister and the Council of Ministers are collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha and are answerable to it through mechanisms like the Question Hour, which require ministers to justify their actions and decisions.
s: States the verdict: False
Correct statement: ministers are answerable to the Lok Sabha, for example through the Question Hour

questions.q: Who is the Head of State and the nominal head of the Executive in India?
questions.a: The President
o: The President
The Prime Minister
The Vice President
The Speaker of the Lok Sabha

questions.q: After an election, a new minister takes charge of a ministry, but most of the officers who run its departments stay the same as before. Which description of these officers in the chapter does this show?
questions.a: They are civil servants, a permanent group working under the direction of ministers
o: They are civil servants, a permanent group working under the direction of ministers
They are members of the Council of Ministers, who are chosen from among the MPs of both houses
They are MPs on a Standing Committee, whose members may change while it remains
They are the Judiciary's officers, who check the Executive's actions

questions.q: The chapter lists the Prime Minister's key functions. Name any two of them.
questions.a: Any two of: leading the Council of Ministers; advising the President; coordinating the work of different ministries; shaping national policies.
s: Names one of: leading the Council of Ministers, advising the President, coordinating ministries, shaping national policies
Names a second, different one of these

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The Prime Minister is the de facto executive authority in India's Parliamentary system.
Reason (R): The President is the Head of State and gives assent to bills.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true

questions.q: A blog post says: 'The Legislature and the Executive are just two names for the same thing, because the President belongs to both.' Test this claim using the chapter's table of differences.
questions.a: Partly right. The President is indeed part of both: the Legislature is the President, the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha, and the Executive is the President, the Vice President and the Council of Ministers. But they are not the same thing: their main roles differ, since the Legislature makes laws and oversees the Executive while the Executive enforces those laws; and in function the Legislature asks questions and sanctions expenses while the Executive explains its actions and prepares and implements the budget.
s: Accepts the overlap: the President is in both compositions
Shows the main roles differ: making laws and overseeing against enforcing laws
Gives one function row that differs (questions and explanations, or sanctioning and implementing the budget) and concludes the claim is only partly right

questions.q:
Two students argue about the President. Riya says: 'The President must be the real decision-maker, because she appoints the Prime Minister and ministers, summons the Parliament and gives assent to bills.' Kabir says: 'The President only attends ceremonies and never has any real choice.' Answer using the chapter.
(a) What two titles does the chapter give the President?
(b) Who actually takes decisions and runs the government?
(c) Which part of Kabir's view is wrong? Give the chapter's example.
(d) Judge which student is closer to the chapter, with a reason.
questions.a: (a) The Head of State and the nominal head of the Executive. (b) The Prime Minister, the de facto executive authority, with the Council of Ministers. (c) 'Never has any real choice' is wrong: in specific circumstances, particularly political crises such as when no party holds a clear majority in a Lok Sabha election, the President can exercise discretionary powers. (d) Kabir is closer on ordinary matters, because the Council of Ministers aids and advises the President and the Prime Minister and ministers run the government; Riya mistakes formal powers for real control. Neither is fully right, since the President's discretion in a crisis is real.
s: (a) Head of State and nominal head of the Executive
(b) The Prime Minister and the Council of Ministers
(c) Discretionary powers in a crisis, such as no clear majority in a Lok Sabha election
(d) Reasoned judgement: Kabir closer on ordinary matters, but neither fully right

questions.q:
Use the chapter's table of differences between the Legislature and the Executive to complete these five lines of a revision chart.
(a) The Legislature is composed of ...
(b) The Executive is composed of ...
(c) The main role of each is ...
(d) Most bills in the Parliament are introduced by ..., while the Legislature can introduce ...
(e) Government-related expenses are sanctioned by ..., and the budget is prepared and implemented by ...
questions.a: (a) The President, the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha. (b) The President, the Vice President, and the Council of Ministers headed by the Prime Minister. (c) The Legislature makes laws and oversees the work of the Executive; the Executive enforces the laws made by the Legislature. (d) The Executive; some bills. (e) The Legislature; the Executive, which implements the budget approved by Parliament.
s: (a) President, Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha
(b) President, Vice President and the Council of Ministers headed by the Prime Minister
(c) Legislature: makes laws and oversees; Executive: enforces laws
(d) The Executive introduces most bills; the Legislature can introduce some
(e) Legislature sanctions expenses; Executive prepares and implements the budget

questions.q: Through what does the Judiciary function, according to the chapter?
questions.a: A system of courts
o: A system of courts
Standing Committees of MPs
The Council of Ministers
The State Assemblies

questions.q: A school poster calls the Judiciary 'the custodian of the Constitution'. Which action below fits that title?
questions.a: Checking that laws passed by Parliament do not violate the Constitutional framework
o: Checking that laws passed by Parliament do not violate the Constitutional framework
Introducing most of the bills that come to the Parliament for discussion
Sanctioning all government-related expenses through the annual budget of Parliament
Electing the President and the Vice President of India

questions.q:
(a) Between which three organs does the chapter describe a system of checks and balances?
(b) What does this system ensure?
questions.a: (a) The Legislature, the Executive and the Judiciary. (b) It ensures that no one organ becomes too powerful.
s: (a) Legislature, Executive and Judiciary
(b) No one organ becomes too powerful

questions.q: A student imagines a country where the Executive both enforces the laws and decides every dispute about how it enforced them. Which risk does the chapter's idea of checks and balances point to?
questions.a: The Executive could become too powerful, with no separate organ checking it against the Constitution
o: The Executive could become too powerful, with no separate organ checking it against the Constitution
Laws would stop needing a vote in the Parliament, since the Executive would now be making all of them
The Legislature would become more powerful, since only it could then question the Executive
Disputes would be settled faster, which the chapter gives as the main aim of separating powers

questions.q: Sanya says: 'If the Judiciary can check the laws that Parliament passes, then the Parliament is no longer the supreme legislative body.' Test her claim.
questions.a: Her claim does not hold. The Parliament is still the body that makes laws for the country; the Judiciary does not make laws but interprets and applies them. The Judiciary's check is only that the laws passed have not violated the Constitutional framework, so Parliament remains the supreme lawmaker within the Constitution, and the check is part of the checks and balances that keep any one organ from becoming too powerful.
s: States that Parliament still makes the laws while the Judiciary interprets and applies them
States that the Judiciary only checks that laws do not violate the Constitutional framework
Concludes the claim fails: Parliament is supreme in lawmaking within the Constitution, and the check is part of checks and balances

questions.q:
An imagined law passed by the Parliament (illustrative) promises every family in a district 20 kg of grain a month, and treats all families alike. In one block of 500 families, the officers of the government department in charge give the grain only to families living in the three villages nearest the block office, and 380 families receive it. The families left out complain that this way of carrying out the law breaks the Constitution.
(a) Which organ made this law?
(b) Which organ is carrying it out?
(c) How many families of the block were left out?
(d) If this way of carrying out the law does violate the Constitution, which organ has the power to step in, and what does the chapter call that organ's role?
questions.a: (a) The Legislature (the Parliament). (b) The Executive. (c) 500 - 380 = 120 families. (d) The Judiciary, which the chapter calls the custodian of the Constitution; it can step in when a violation of the Constitution occurs as the Executive implements a law.
s: (a) The Legislature / Parliament
(b) The Executive
(c) 120 families
(d) The Judiciary, custodian of the Constitution

questions.q: Four students describe the legislature of their own state. Whose description agrees with the chapter?
questions.a: Meera from Telangana: 'We have a Vidhan Sabha and a Vidhan Parishad.'
o: Meera from Telangana: 'We have a Vidhan Sabha and a Vidhan Parishad.'
Arif from Rajasthan: 'Our state has a Vidhan Parishad as its upper house.'
Lina from Karnataka: 'Our state has only one house, the Vidhan Sabha.'

questions.q: Differentiate between a unicameral and a bicameral state legislature, naming the house or houses that each has.
questions.a: A unicameral state legislature has only one house, the Vidhan Sabha (legislative assembly). A bicameral one has two houses: the Vidhan Sabha and the Vidhan Parishad (legislative council, the upper house).
s: Unicameral: one house, the Vidhan Sabha
Bicameral: two houses, the Vidhan Sabha and the Vidhan Parishad (upper house)

questions.q: A state minister says: 'Education is in the Concurrent List, so my state may choose not to follow the RTE Act.' True or false: the minister is right. Give the reason or the correct statement.
questions.a: False. On a Concurrent List subject, if the Union government legislates, the state government is bound to follow it; that is why the RTE Act applies all over India even though education is in the Concurrent List.
s: States the verdict: False
Correct statement: once the Union legislates on a Concurrent List subject the state is bound to follow, so RTE applies all over India

questions.q:
In an imagined state (illustrative) with both a Vidhan Sabha and a Vidhan Parishad, a coalition of three parties holds the majority in the Vidhan Sabha after an election. Using the chapter's table of union and state structures, answer:
(a) Whose leader becomes the de facto executive authority of the state, and what is that office called?
(b) Who selects the state's Council of Ministers?
(c) To which house is that Council collectively responsible, even though the state has two houses?
questions.a: (a) The leader of the majority coalition in the Vidhan Sabha becomes the Chief Minister, the de facto executive authority of the state. (b) The Chief Minister. (c) The Vidhan Sabha, not the Vidhan Parishad, just as the Union Council is responsible to the Lok Sabha.
s: (a) Leader of the majority coalition in the Vidhan Sabha, as Chief Minister
(b) The Chief Minister selects it
(c) Collectively responsible to the Vidhan Sabha

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Every state in India has a bicameral legislature, just like the Centre.
Reason (R): In a state with two houses, the legislative council, or upper house, is called the Vidhan Parishad.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: A is false, but R is true
o: A is false, but R is true
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false

questions.q:
Telangana is one of the states named in the chapter. Suppose (illustrative) its legislature passes a law on a subject in the Concurrent List, and two years later the Parliament passes a different law on the same subject.
(a) Is Telangana's legislature unicameral or bicameral? Name its house or houses.
(b) Could Telangana's MLAs make a law on this subject at all? Give the chapter's rule.
(c) Which law must the state follow after the Parliament's law, and why?
(d) If the state's law had needed a new tax, in which house could that money bill originate?
(e) The chapter says matters like education need collaboration between the union and the states, showing the 'interdependent nature of federalism'. Explain this with the RTE example.
questions.a: (a) Bicameral: the Vidhan Sabha and the Vidhan Parishad. (b) Yes: MLAs formulate laws on subjects in the State List and the Concurrent List. (c) The Parliament's law, because when the Union legislates on a Concurrent List subject the state government is bound to follow it. (d) Only in the Vidhan Sabha. (e) Education is in the Concurrent List, so both levels can legislate on it; RTE was passed by the Parliament and applies all over India, so every state works within the same Union law. Neither level acts alone on such a subject, which is why the chapter calls federalism interdependent.
s: (a) Bicameral: Vidhan Sabha and Vidhan Parishad
(b) Yes, MLAs legislate on State and Concurrent List subjects
(c) The Parliament's law, as states are bound to follow a Union law on a Concurrent subject
(d) The Vidhan Sabha only
(e) RTE: a Union law on a Concurrent subject applies in every state, so the two levels depend on each other

questions.a: With equal sessions, the 13th Lok Sabha had 321 fewer sittings, so fewer sittings per session

questions.q:
An imagined session (illustrative) of the Parliament has 22 sittings, each of the usual length the chapter gives.
(a) For how many hours was the House scheduled to function in this session?
(b) If it actually functioned for 88 hours, what was its productivity, to the nearest whole per cent?
questions.a: (a) The Parliament usually sits 6 hours a day, so 22 x 6 = 132 hours. (b) 88 / 132 x 100 = 66.7, so about 67 per cent.
s: (a) 22 x 6 = 132 hours scheduled
(b) 88 / 132 x 100, about 67 per cent

questions.q:
Read the notes from one week of an imagined House (illustrative). Monday: a large number of members did not attend. Tuesday: the Question Hour was lost to shouting. Wednesday: an important bill was passed after only eight minutes of debate.
(a) Name the challenge from the chapter that Monday shows.
(b) Name the challenge that Wednesday shows.
(c) Which day's problem most directly weakens the Executive's accountability to the House? Explain why.
questions.a: (a) Regular absenteeism of members. (b) Reduced quality of important debates. (c) Tuesday: the Question Hour is the time when MPs ask ministers about government policies and activities and ministers must justify their actions, so disrupting it removes a main way of holding the Executive accountable.
s: (a) Absenteeism of members
(b) Reduced quality of important debates
(c) Tuesday, because the Question Hour is where ministers must justify their actions to MPs

questions.q:
An imagined State Assembly (illustrative) holds a Monsoon Session of 12 sittings, each scheduled for 6 hours. It actually functions for 30 hours in all. The Question Hour is disrupted on 8 of the 12 days. Of the 9 bills listed for the session, 6 are passed, each after less than 10 minutes of debate. The Assembly's office announces: 'Six of nine bills passed, so the session was a success.'
(a) How many hours was the session scheduled for, and what was its productivity, to one decimal place?
(b) On what fraction of the days was the Question Hour disrupted?
(c) Name two challenges from the chapter that this data shows.
(d) Judge the office's claim, using the data and the chapter's view of what legislatures are meant to be.
questions.a: (a) 12 x 6 = 72 hours; 30 / 72 x 100 = 41.7 per cent. (b) 8 / 12 = two-thirds of the days. (c) Disruptions of the Question Hour, and reduced quality of important debates (bills passed in under 10 minutes). (d) The claim is weak: passing two-thirds of the listed bills is something, but the House functioned for well under half its scheduled time, lost the Question Hour on two-thirds of days and passed bills almost without debate. The chapter sees legislatures as spaces for thoughtful debate where laws are made in the people's interest, so counting bills passed alone overstates the session's success.
s: (a) 72 hours scheduled; productivity 41.7 per cent
(b) Two-thirds (8 of 12) of the days
(c) Question Hour disruptions and reduced quality of debates
(d) Judges the claim weak, weighing bills passed against low productivity, lost Question Hours and hurried debate

questions.q:
Answer briefly.
(a) Name any two challenges to the effective functioning of the legislatures, as listed in the chapter.
(b) For how many hours a day does the Parliament usually sit during a session?
(c) Name one thing the chapter says citizens can do to help overcome these challenges.
questions.a: (a) Any two of: regular absenteeism of members; non-cooperative conduct or communication of members; reduced quality of important debates; disruptions of the Question Hour. (b) 6 hours, which can be extended on special occasions or for urgent business. (c) Any one of: stay informed on matters of importance to society; participate in public debate on the digital spaces that government departments offer during policymaking; constructively engage with political representatives on policies.
s: (a) Two of: absenteeism, non-cooperative conduct, reduced quality of debates, Question Hour disruptions
(b) 6 hours a day
(c) One citizen action: stay informed, join public debate on digital spaces, or engage constructively with representatives
